content: Beclomethasone dipropionate (BDP) and budesonide (BUD) are widely used inhaled corticosteroids for managing asthma. Fluticasone propionate (FP) is a newer corticosteroid with greater potency demonstrated in laboratory studies. The purpose of this review was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of fluticasone compared to beclomethasone or budesonide in treating chronic asthma. Randomized trials involving both children and adults were included in the analysis. A comprehensive search was conducted, including databases, reference lists, and abstracts from major respiratory society meetings. Additional data were sought from trial authors and pharmaceutical companies. A total of 71 studies, involving 14,602 participants and 74 randomized comparisons, met the inclusion criteria. The methodological quality of the studies was deemed fair. The analysis compared fluticasone to beclomethasone or budesonide at two dose ratios: 1:2 (fluticasone at half the dose of beclomethasone or budesonide) and 1:1 (equal doses of fluticasone and the comparator drugs). When fluticasone was administered at half the dose of beclomethasone or budesonide (1:2 dose ratio), it resulted in a statistically significant improvement in end-of-treatment forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) by 0.04 liters (95% confidence interval: 0 to 0.07 liters). Improvements were also observed in morning peak expiratory flow (PEF) at the end of treatment. However, there were no significant differences in changes in FEV1 or evening PEF. These findings were consistent across all age groups, drug doses, and delivery devices. Fluticasone at this dose ratio was associated with fewer asthma symptoms and reduced use of rescue medication. However, it was linked to a higher likelihood of pharyngitis (sore throat) compared to beclomethasone or budesonide. There was no significant difference in the risk of oral candidiasis between the drugs. When fluticasone was given at the same dose as beclomethasone or budesonide (1:1 dose ratio), it showed statistically significant improvements in morning PEF, evening PEF, and FEV1 compared to the other two drugs. The effects on asthma exacerbations were inconsistent across studies. There were no significant differences in the incidence of hoarseness, pharyngitis, oral candidiasis, or cough between fluticasone and the comparator drugs. Plasma cortisol and 24-hour urinary cortisol levels were frequently measured in the studies, but the data were not consistently presented. This limited the ability to draw conclusions about the effects of fluticasone on adrenal function. However, there are concerns about potential adrenal suppression in children receiving fluticasone at doses greater than 400 mcg/day. The included trials did not provide sufficient data to address this issue comprehensively. In conclusion, fluticasone, when administered at half the daily dose of beclomethasone or budesonide, leads to modest improvements in airway function but carries a higher risk of sore throat. At equivalent doses, fluticasone may increase the risk of hoarseness. Further research is needed to clarify the potential for adrenal suppression, particularly in children receiving higher doses of fluticasone.
